doc.title: Pete Barbutti interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 8, 2022

title: Rafael Mendez sits in at Rosellini's 410, Seattle
summary: Mendez played Tico Tico on his trumpet; later dedicated a solo at the Roy Rogers show while the kids rode Trigger.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Yeah. I have to tell you, in fact one of the great stories of my life, I’m working a club in Seattle. This was right after Spokane. It was the year of the World’s Fair in 1962. I have a

great trio behind me and I’m working this little club called Rosellini’s 410. It was a very hip place, and it was packed every night. I’m working it and somebody sends up a note that says, “Rafael Mendez is in the audience.” And I said well it’s somebody named Rafael Mendez but obviously it’s not THE Rafael Mendez, he’s the greatest classical trumpet player that ever lived. And from the back of the room I hear, “Yeah he’s here.” I said, “What’s he doing here?” “He’s conducting the orchestra out at the fairgrounds for the big show, the Roy Rogers show.” It was a big orchestra and Rafael Mendez was doing a song and, you know. I said my God Rafael Mendez is in the audience, “Ladies and gentlemen, the greatest trumpetist who’s ever lived.” And some drunk yelled, “Have him sit in.” And with that I chastised this drunk, said, “Sir you don’t understand. Rafael Mendez is above what we’re all doing or thinking here. He is on a level —” And Rafael Mendez said, “Yeah I don’t mind.” He gets up, he takes my old beat-up trumpet, he turns to the trio and says, “‘Tico Tico’ in A minor.” He does double, triple tonguing and then he does a chorus of the circular breathing where he never breathes and then he goes — and he ends it on a double A above high C, which was like a B on trumpet, almost a double C. Then he hands me the trumpet and gets off the stage, while I stand there looking at the trumpet and the laughs start, and I keep looking at it and I look up at him and the laugh gets bigger and I look at the band and they all go like this and the laugh gets bigger you know. And I look at the trumpet again, examine it you know, and the laughs just kept getting bigger and bigger. It’s like what the hell am I going to do with this thing there’s nothing left. Every note in the world has been played. And finally I put the trumpet down and I got a round of applause like it was the longest laugh I’ve ever had in my life. And then I took the kids out, the three because the young one was too little. I took the kids and I had them fly up to Seattle because I was there for a long time, my wife and the kids. And I took them out because Rafael Mendez said, “Come on” he was Roy Rogers’ manager, Art Rush was his manager for like 30 years, never had a contract, never had an argument, he was a wonderful, kind man. Art Rush said, “Bring your family out to see Roy Rogers in the show.” So I took them out and I met Art Rush there and he gave me a nice hug, and these are my three kids. He said, “I bet the kids would like to ride on Trigger.” He brought Trigger out, who was old at the time. And put the kids on Trigger and they rode around a little bit. And I said wow this is really something, I mean if you grew up in our generation Roy Rogers and Trigger, that was you’re talking about legends. So then we go up in the stands and in the middle of the show Rafael Mendez says I’d like to do this solo trumpet piece, whatever he was going to do. He says, “I’d like to dedicate it to my buddy Pete Barbutti, another great trumpet player in the stands,” and everybody applauded. I said, “Did you hear that?” And the kids said to me, “Yeah, Dad, but we rode Trigger.” I thought yeah, everything is relative.
